match.reason: No point in the bank covers how changes in the Australian dollar affect export and import prices; the closest one, on economic and financial influences, is broader and does not teach exchange rate effects.

draft.title: Exchange rates and international business
card: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, such as how many US dollars one Australian dollar buys. It can rise or fall over time.
Overseas buyers need more of their own currency to buy Australian goods, so exports become dearer to them. Australians pay less in AUD for foreign goods, so imports become cheaper.
Exports become cheaper for overseas buyers and imports become dearer for Australians. This is the opposite of a rise.
Exchange rate changes alter what overseas sales are worth. If an exporter is paid in a foreign currency, a higher AUD turns that payment into fewer Australian dollars.
draft.remember: A higher AUD makes exports dearer and imports cheaper. A lower AUD does the reverse.

a.q: The Australian dollar rises against the Japanese yen. What is the likely effect on a Sydney importer buying goods priced in yen?
opts: The goods cost fewer Australian dollars
The goods cost more Australian dollars
The goods cost the same in Australian dollars
The goods cost fewer yen for Japanese buyers
a.why: A higher AUD buys more yen, so a yen-priced invoice costs fewer Australian dollars. The tempting option about more dollars reverses the effect and treats a rise as if it were a fall.
a.clue: A stronger AUD buys more of the foreign currency.

b.q: Kira's winery in the Barossa Valley sells wine to the United States and is paid in US dollars. The AUD rises against the USD. What is the likely effect on her?
opts: Each USD payment is worth fewer Australian dollars
Each USD payment is worth more Australian dollars
US buyers find her wine cheaper in their currency
Her wine costs less to make in Australia
b.why: When the AUD rises, each US dollar buys fewer Australian dollars, so her sales are worth less when converted. The option about more dollars is tempting because a rise sounds like good news, but a higher AUD makes exports dearer for buyers.
b.clue: Think about what each US dollar converts into after the AUD rises.

a.best: The goods cost fewer Australian dollars

b.best: Each USD payment is worth fewer Australian dollars

problems.detail: The why's second sentence rebuts the 'more Australian dollars' distractor by saying a higher AUD makes exports dearer for buyers. That is true, but it does not explain the conversion effect the distractor is about. It could confuse students about why the payment converts into fewer AUD. The why should say instead that each USD now buys fewer AUD.
